Billie Holiday was an American jazz vocalist whose intimate phrasing and emotional depth made her one of the greatest interpreters of jazz standards. She had a distinctive contralto voice known for subtle rhythmic phrasing. She sang slightly behind the beat, creating an intimate, conversational quality that drew listeners into her world.

In 1939, she recorded "Strange Fruit," a searing protest against lynching. This recording established the jazz standard as a powerful vehicle for social commentary and emotional truth. She collaborated closely with saxophonist Lester Young, developing an almost telepathic interplay between them. His nickname was Prez and hers was Lady Day, reflecting the mutual respect they shared.

Her signature interpretations included "God Bless the Child," "Don't Explain," and "The Very Thought of You," each showcasing her ability to mine emotional depths and subtle harmonic implications. Throughout her career, she faced struggles with addiction and racial discrimination, yet these hardships informed her tragic dignity and emotional authenticity in performance. She influenced generations of jazz and popular singers who learned that song interpretation required vulnerability and personal investment.
